sources.label: GloVe 6B 300d
sources.blurb: Stanford, 2014, trained on 6 billion tokens of Wikipedia. Single words only — but this is the model king − man + woman was discovered on, and the arithmetic still works.
sources.cross_lingual_note: English Wikipedia and Gigaword, nothing else. It has a vector for 'agua' only because English text sometimes contains 'agua', and that vector is placed by the English company the word keeps — not by what it means in Spanish. Half the translations word set is outside its vocabulary entirely.

sources.label: OpenAI text-embedding-3-small
sources.blurb: The default modern choice. 1536 dimensions, understands phrases and sentences, costs about $0.02 per million tokens.
sources.cross_lingual_note: Multilingual, and OpenAI does not publish the recipe or the language count. It retrieves translations reliably; it also keeps a visible amount of the language itself in the vector.

sources.label: OpenAI text-embedding-3-large
sources.blurb: Twice the dimensions of 3-small and measurably better at retrieval. Twice as many numbers to flatten into three, too.
sources.cross_lingual_note: The larger sibling, and — on the translations set — the more language-sensitive of the two. Bigger is not the same as more language-agnostic.

sources.label: Cohere embed-multilingual-v3.0
sources.blurb: 100+ languages behind an HTTP API, L2-normalised at 1024 dimensions, and the only model here that asks what the vectors are for: these are clustering embeddings, not search ones.
sources.cross_lingual_note: Cohere documents cross-lingual retrieval as a headline capability — a Chinese query against Finnish documents — but publishes no paper and no training recipe, so on evidence it files with the merely multilingual models rather than beside LaBSE and MiniLM, whose objectives are written down. Measured, it sits exactly there, and not at the top: its mean same-meaning cosine of 0.793 is below LaBSE's and e5's, and its gap of +0.174 is fifth of eight. What it leads on is separability among the merely multilingual — concept silhouette +0.480, AUC 0.943, best-cutoff F1 0.917 — while its silhouette *by language* stays *positive* at +0.052, where every translation-trained model goes negative. It retrieves every translation without having been taught to forget which language it was in, which is a property rather than a virtue: it is what you want for language-aware search and the wrong thing for language-blind search.

sources.label: multilingual-e5-small
sources.blurb: 118M parameters, 100 languages, runs on the CPU in front of you. A general multilingual retriever rather than a translation model.
sources.cross_lingual_note: Contrastively pretrained on a billion mined multilingual pairs, then fine-tuned for retrieval. Never given a translation dictionary. It ranks translations first and still puts every pair of strings above 0.8 — which is why retrieval accuracy and the same-meaning gap have to be read together.

sources.label: paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2
sources.blurb: 118M parameters, 50 languages, 384 dimensions. Distilled so that a translation lands where the English original already was.
sources.cross_lingual_note: Multilingual knowledge distillation (Reimers & Gurevych, 2020): a monolingual English teacher embedded a sentence, and the student was trained to put that sentence *and its translations* at the same coordinates. Cross-lingual alignment is not a side effect here, it is the loss function.

sources.label: BGE-M3
sources.blurb: 568M parameters, 100+ languages, an 8192-token context. The current strong multilingual retriever, and the largest model here.
sources.cross_lingual_note: BAAI, 2024. Trained on a mixture that includes mined parallel text with cross-lingual retrieval as a stated objective, so it belongs with the aligned models rather than the merely multilingual ones — but it is a retrieval model first and a translation model second, which is the interesting difference between it and LaBSE.

sources.label: LaBSE
sources.blurb: 471M parameters, 109 languages. Trained on 6 billion translation pairs — the reference model for finding a sentence's translation.
sources.cross_lingual_note: Language-agnostic BERT Sentence Embedding (Feng et al., 2020). Trained with an additive-margin softmax over 6B translation pairs, which pushes a sentence and its translation together and every other pair apart. If any model here should make language invisible, it is this one.

sources.label: GloVe 6B 300d, translated first
sources.blurb: Every word translated to English, then embedded by GloVe 6B 300d. The query gets translated too, so the whole index is monolingual and any English model can serve it.
sources.cross_lingual_note: Cross-lingual retrieval without a cross-lingual model: translate the documents to English, translate the query to English, and let an English index do the work. The model's own language coverage stops mattering — what matters instead is the translator, and everything the original wording carried that a translation does not.

presets.label: Royalty and gender
presets.blurb: The classic. Pairs that differ only in gender, plus the titles that go with them.
presets.look_for: The pairs should sit parallel: the arrow from man to woman points the same way as the one from king to queen. That parallelism is what makes king − man + woman work at all.

presets.label: Countries and capitals
presets.blurb: Nine countries next to the cities that run them.
presets.look_for: Countries cluster with countries and cities with cities, but the country-to-capital offset is roughly constant — so paris − france + japan lands near tokyo.

presets.label: Six unrelated fields
presets.blurb: Fruit, vehicles, instruments, emotions, weather and colours, shuffled together.
presets.look_for: The one set where every method agrees. Six clumps should fall out without being told there are six — the structure is in the vectors, not in the colouring.

presets.label: Words with two meanings
presets.blurb: bank, bat, apple, python, mercury — each with the company both of its senses keep.
presets.look_for: A word has exactly one vector, so a word with two meanings gets stranded between them. Watch 'python' sit halfway between the snakes and the programming, belonging to neither.

presets.label: Tense and inflection
presets.blurb: The same verbs in every form they take.
presets.look_for: Grammar has a geometry. The step from walk to walking is close to the step from swim to swimming, which is why the arithmetic works on conjugation as well as on meaning.

presets.label: Good, better, best
presets.blurb: Adjectives with their comparative and superlative forms.
presets.look_for: Three loose shelves — base, -er, -est — with each word's own meaning deciding where it sits along the shelf. Intensity and grammar are two separate directions in the same space.

presets.label: Opposites
presets.blurb: Antonym pairs, which embeddings are famously bad at separating.
presets.look_for: hot and cold come out as near neighbours. Nothing is broken: they are used in the same sentences about the same things, and these models encode context, not truth. Opposites are a known blind spot.

presets.label: Sentences, not words
presets.blurb: Paraphrase pairs and one intruder. Needs a model that embeds sentences.
presets.look_for: This is what the OpenAI models were actually built for. Each pair says the same thing in different words and should land almost on top of itself, while the topic changes sit far apart. GloVe cannot do this at all — it has no vector for a sentence.
words: the cat sat on the mat
a feline rested on a rug
the dog barked at the postman
a hound howled at the mail carrier
set the oven at 200C before baking
my flight has been delayed again
the plane is running late once more

presets.label: One string, two languages
presets.blurb: Eight strings that are ordinary words in both English and German, meaning unrelated things, each with the English word for both of its senses.
presets.look_for: The limit of the whole idea. A model is handed a string, not a language, so 'gift' gets exactly one vector to cover an English present and a German poison. Check each trio: is the string nearer its English sense or its German one? English wins seven of eight on GloVe, on OpenAI 3-small and on minilm-multilingual, and eight of eight on LaBSE — so the exceptions are the interesting part. The word models both read 'kind' as the German for child rather than the English for caring, and minilm-multilingual reads 'gut' as the German for good at 0.83 against 0.23 for intestine. The more languages a model knows, the more ways there are for a bare string to be ambiguous, and nothing in the input can resolve it.

presets.label: Numbers and time
presets.blurb: Digits, number words, days and months.
presets.look_for: Ordered things often come out as an arc or a line rather than a blob. Look for the days of the week in order — the model was never told they have an order.

presets.label: The same word in six languages
presets.blurb: Eight everyday concepts — water, dog, house, book, mother, bread, sun, moon — in English, French, Spanish, German, Russian and Hindi.
presets.look_for: Colour by language, then by meaning, and see which one the plot was already sorted by. On GloVe the languages separate and the concepts do not; on LaBSE the eight concepts fall into eight groups of six and the languages are nowhere. Then find the French 'pain' — spelled like the English word for suffering, and the one point where form and meaning disagree. LaBSE puts it with 'хлеб'; GloVe puts it with 'mother'; and minilm-multilingual, which otherwise wins this set, puts it with 'sol'.

presets.label: Eight writing systems
presets.blurb: Five concepts, eight languages, and no two of them written in the same alphabet.
presets.look_for: The hardest version of the question. A tokeniser sees characters, and nothing about 水 and 물 and وشمس looks alike at that level — so any model that groups these by meaning is doing it despite the surface, not because of it. This is also where GloVe stops being wrong and starts being absent: it has no vector for a single non-Latin character string at all.

presets.label: The same sentence in six languages
presets.blurb: Four sentences, each translated five times. Needs a model that embeds sentences.
presets.look_for: Sentences are what these encoders were trained on, so this is the kindest test in the app and the scores should be the highest you see. A sentence gives the model far more to work with than a bare noun does — there is grammar, tense and topic in it, and all of that survives translation. If a model is going to make language invisible anywhere, it is here.

the train leaves at nine in the morning
le train part à neuf heures du matin
el tren sale a las nueve de la mañana
der Zug fährt um neun Uhr morgens ab
поезд отходит в девять часов утра
ट्रेन सुबह नौ बजे निकलती है

elle aime lire des livres le soir
le encanta leer libros por la tarde

methods.label: PCA
methods.blurb: Linear. The three directions the words vary along most.
methods.detail: Principal component analysis rotates the space so the first axis is the direction of greatest variance, then the second, then the third, and throws the rest away. It is linear, instant and completely deterministic — the same words always give the same picture. The cost shows up in the variance readout: three axes out of 1536 typically retain 10-30% of the variation, so most of what distinguishes these words has been discarded to fit them on a screen. Distances you see are real but heavily compressed, and unrelated words can land on top of each other because they happen to agree on three axes.

methods.label: t-SNE
methods.blurb: Neighbourhoods only. Beautiful clusters, meaningless gaps.
methods.detail: t-SNE converts distances into probabilities of being neighbours, then arranges points in 3-D so those probabilities match as closely as it can. It is very good at what it promises and routinely misread. Two things are true and worth holding onto: points inside a clump really are near each other in the original space, and the distance between two clumps is an artefact of the layout. A large gap does not mean the groups are unrelated. Perplexity is roughly 'how many neighbours count' — raise it and clusters merge, lower it and they shatter.

params.label: Perplexity
params.hint: Roughly how many neighbours each point tries to stay near.

methods.label: UMAP
methods.blurb: Neighbourhoods plus some global shape. Usually the best picture.
methods.detail: UMAP builds a graph of each point's nearest neighbours and then finds a 3-D layout of that graph. In practice it keeps t-SNE's clean local clusters while preserving more of the relationship between them, which makes it the one to reach for when you want a single view. It is also the hardest to argue about: the layout depends on the graph, and the graph depends on n_neighbors. Low values give many small islands, high values pull everything into one continent.

params.label: Neighbours
params.hint: Small values favour local detail, large values global shape.

params.label: Min distance
params.hint: How tightly points may be packed together.

methods.label: MDS
methods.blurb: Matches real cosine distances as closely as three axes allow.
methods.detail: Multidimensional scaling takes the full table of true cosine distances and looks for the 3-D arrangement whose straight-line distances match it best. That makes it the only method on this list whose picture you are allowed to measure: if two words look twice as far apart as two others, they roughly are. The honesty has a price — it reports the residual disagreement as stress, and on real embedding data the stress is high, because the geometry genuinely does not fit in three dimensions. Below about 0.1 is a good fit, above 0.2 means the distances on screen are only suggestive.

methods.label: Random projection
methods.blurb: Three random directions. The control condition.
methods.detail: Multiply the vectors by a random matrix and keep three of the results. This is not a straw man: the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma says random projection preserves distances remarkably well — into a few hundred dimensions. Into three it collapses into a blob, which is the useful part. Flip between this and UMAP on the same words: everything you can see in one and not the other is what the method contributed, rather than something that was lying around in the data.

methods.label: Raw dimensions
methods.blurb: Three dimensions of the actual vector, chosen by index or by variance.
methods.detail: No reduction at all — just three dimensions of the raw vector as x, y and z. The result is noise, and that is the lesson. Unlike the columns of a spreadsheet, a single dimension of a learned embedding has no meaning of its own; the information lives in the combination of all of them. Switching the picker to the most varied dimensions is the fair version of the test — instead of arbitrary indices it hands raw mode the three best dimensions available for these particular words, and the readout prints what they explain against what three PCA components explain. On LaBSE with the translations set that is 1.1% against 46.1%, so the best three dimensions in the model lose to three learned combinations by a factor of forty. That ratio is the whole reason the other five methods exist, and it is worth having as a number rather than an assertion.

params.label: Pick by
params.hint: index uses the sliders; most varied uses the three dimensions that differ most across the words on screen

glossary.label: embedding
glossary.short: A list of a few hundred to a few thousand numbers standing in for a word or a sentence, learned so that similar meanings get similar lists.
glossary.detail: Every model here turns text into one fixed-length list of numbers. The numbers are not features anyone chose — they came out of training — so no single one of them means anything on its own. What they carry is relative: the interesting question is never what a vector *is* but which other vectors it is near.

glossary.label: cosine similarity
glossary.short: The angle between two vectors, as a number from -1 to 1. 1 is the same direction, 0 is unrelated.
glossary.detail: Cosine ignores how long the vectors are and compares only their direction, which is what you want when one word appeared a million times in training and another appeared a thousand. Every similarity in this app is a cosine computed on the full vectors — never on the three coordinates a projection produced. In practice fewer than 2% of real word pairs come out negative, so the colour ramp starts at 0 and the theoretical floor of -1 is never reached.

glossary.label: dimension
glossary.short: One position in the list. Individually meaningless: there is no 'water dimension'.
glossary.detail: The raw projection method exists to demonstrate this. On LaBSE the three most varied dimensions out of 768 account for 1.1% of the variation between words, where three PCA components — learned combinations of all 768 — account for 46.1%. But the *set* of dimensions a word drives hardest is partly shared by its translations: `water` and `вода` share all five of their top five, `book` and `livre` share one. Across the translations grid the rank correlation between that overlap and cosine has a median of +0.53 — real, and loose. So meaning is spread across a combination rather than stored in any one place, and the combination is still partly legible. Both halves are measured: the first by raw mode, the second by the dimensions panel.

glossary.label: hub dimension
glossary.short: A dimension that is large for almost every word, carrying a global offset rather than anything about the word.
glossary.detail: These models have a handful of dimensions — sometimes called rogue or hub dimensions — with a large value for nearly every input. Dimension 216 is in the top five of `water`, `dog` and `book` on LaBSE. Ranking a word's dimensions by raw size therefore mostly returns hubs, which is the most convincing wrong answer in the area. Ranking by distance from the mean removes them for free, because a dimension that is large for everyone deviates for no one — but it removes much of the real signal with them, so the dimensions panel flags hubs instead of subtracting them, and also reports the overlap with them deleted so you can see what they were worth. How much they matter differs sharply by model: bge-m3 has five of them where multilingual-e5-small has none.

glossary.label: input type
glossary.short: Cohere's embed v3 makes you declare what the vector is for. The same string embedded for search and for clustering comes back as two different vectors.
glossary.detail: Asymmetric search needs a three-word query and a three-paragraph document to land near each other, so `search_query` and `search_document` are trained to be read against each other rather than against themselves. Every number in this app is a cosine between two items drawn from the same pool — the similarity matrix, k-means, the silhouette, the translation retrieval — which is the symmetric case, so the Cohere source asks for `clustering` and never asks for anything else. Two input types in one index would be two subtly different geometries in one collection, and no error would ever be raised about it. It is the same kind of decision as the `query: ` prefix multilingual-e5 was trained with, or the pooling an ONNX export leaves to whoever runs it: not configuration, part of what the model means. The other models here take the choice away by having only one mode — which is a smaller API and a quieter assumption, not a better one.

glossary.label: projection
glossary.short: Any way of turning hundreds of dimensions into the three a screen has. All of them lose information; they differ in what they lose.
glossary.detail: There is no faithful picture of a 768-dimensional cloud in three dimensions, so the question is never whether a projection lied but which lie it told. That is why every view here carries trustworthiness and distance correlation, and why the random projection is offered as a control: it shows what no method at all looks like, so the others can be judged against something.

glossary.label: trustworthiness
glossary.short: Of each point's nearest neighbours on screen, how many were genuinely among its nearest in full dimensions. Higher is better.
glossary.detail: This is the neighbourhood question: can you trust that two dots drawn close together really are close in the model? It says nothing about distances — t-SNE routinely scores well here while getting every distance wrong, which is exactly t-SNE's signature and the most misread property of these plots. Read it next to distance correlation, never alone.

glossary.label: distance correlation
glossary.short: Rank correlation between every true cosine distance and the distance actually drawn. Higher means the picture is measurable.
glossary.detail: Where trustworthiness asks about neighbours, this asks whether the gaps mean anything — whether a cloud twice as far away is twice as unrelated. MDS optimises this directly and scores highest; t-SNE scores around 0.37 on the six-field word set, which is why the distance between two t-SNE clusters should never be read as meaningful. A random projection scores about 0.01, which is the floor.

glossary.label: explained variance
glossary.short: The share of the spread between these words that the three drawn axes actually account for.
glossary.detail: PCA reports this honestly and it is usually lower than people expect — 10 to 30% for three components on real embeddings. The raw method reports it too, alongside what three PCA components would have managed on the same words, which turns 'raw dimensions are noise' from an assertion into a ratio you can read.

glossary.label: stress
glossary.short: MDS's own residual: how much disagreement is left between true and drawn distances. Lower is better.
glossary.detail: MDS works by minimising exactly this, so stress is the one quality number here reported by the method about its own objective rather than measured from outside. It is why MDS is the only layout in the app whose axes you may sensibly measure with a ruler.

glossary.label: anchoring
glossary.short: Rotating a new layout onto the previous one, so adding a word does not spin the whole cloud.
glossary.detail: t-SNE and UMAP have no preferred orientation: the same data can come out mirrored or rotated on a second run, and none of that carries information. Each new frame is therefore fitted onto the last by orthogonal Procrustes, which removes the part of a change that is arbitrary and leaves the part that is real.

glossary.label: group
glossary.short: k-means run on the full vectors, not on the three coordinates — so the colouring is independent evidence, not a restatement.
glossary.detail: Because the grouping is computed in full dimensions and the positions come from the projection, a group that also lands together on screen is two independent readings agreeing. If the colours were derived from the coordinates, the plot would be confirming itself. Colour carries the group up to three of them; past that, marker shape does, because no six hues in the lightness band a dark surface needs stay distinguishable to a colour-blind viewer.

glossary.label: cross-lingual
glossary.short: Whether a model puts a word near its translations. It takes deliberate training; it does not come free with seeing many languages.
glossary.detail: A monolingual model has no reason to put `agua` near `water` — it saw `agua` in English sentences about Spanish, so it learned a vector meaning 'a Spanish-looking word'. Language is a stronger signal in text than meaning is. The sources here are tagged by how they came by the ability: none, incidental, multilingual (many languages, never told which strings are translations) and aligned (translation pairs as an explicit objective). The tag predicts the measurements better than parameter count does.

glossary.label: translation found
glossary.short: Of the words in other languages, how often the nearest one is this word's own translation.
glossary.detail: The retrieval question, and the one a search index lives on. It is also the easiest to over-read: a model can score 100% here and still be useless for setting a similarity threshold, because ranking correctly says nothing about the margin. multilingual-e5-small scores 100% with a margin of 0.06. Always read it beside the margin, and check the list of misses — 94% with a hard case among the misses is a different model from 94% without.

glossary.label: margin
glossary.short: Mean same-meaning similarity minus mean same-language similarity. How much meaning wins by, rather than whether it wins.
glossary.detail: This is what a similarity cutoff in a real system gets set against. GloVe's is negative on the translations grid, meaning words of the same language are on average closer than translations of each other. A model with a compressed cosine range is punished here for something a user may not care about, which is why the scale-free version is reported next to it.

glossary.label: meaning beats language
glossary.short: Every translation pair compared against every same-language pair, counting how often meaning is closer. 50% is a coin flip.
glossary.detail: The scale-free version of the margin: it only asks which pair is closer, never by how much, so a model that squashes all its cosines into a narrow band is not penalised for it. Between this and the margin you can tell a model that ranks well and calibrates badly from one that does neither.

glossary.label: silhouette
glossary.short: How well a labelling fits the geometry. Computed twice — by concept and by language — and the higher one is what the space is sorted by.
glossary.detail: The only number here that can come out negative, which is the interesting case: it means real clusters exist and the label you gave them is the wrong one. GloVe scores negative by concept and positive by language, so the clusters in GloVe's space are languages. LaBSE is the other way round. Reading the two against each other is the whole question in one comparison.

glossary.label: cohesion
glossary.short: How tightly one concept holds together across languages. The loosest concepts are the informative ones.
glossary.detail: A concept with low cohesion is usually one whose translations are not quite synonyms, or one containing a word that is spelled like something else — which is more useful to know than the average.

glossary.label: translate first
glossary.short: Translate every document and every query to English, then run an ordinary English index. The other way to build multilingual search.
glossary.detail: It costs a translation call per document and per query and throws the original wording away, but afterwards every vector is an English vector — so even a 2014 English-only word model retrieves across languages. Asking a translate-first GloVe index for the neighbours of `собака` returns `dogs, cat, pet, puppy, hound` out of the full 50,000-word English vocabulary. The model's language coverage stops mattering and the translator's quality starts.

glossary.label: collapse
glossary.short: When translation turns several documents into the same string, so the index holds one vector where the word set had several.
glossary.detail: A dictionary turns `eau`, `agua`, `Wasser`, `вода` and `पानी` all into the literal string `water`. The model returns one vector for one string, so six documents become one and every score goes to a perfect 1.000 — by arithmetic, not by skill, because there is nothing left to retrieve across. The comparison reports this instead of the scores when it happens. It is a real finding and it cuts both ways: translation erases the language, and it erases the difference between the documents with it. Sentences are where the comparison becomes meaningful, because their translations are not byte-identical.

glossary.label: homograph
glossary.short: One spelling that is a word in two languages with unrelated meanings. A model gets a string, not a language.
glossary.detail: `gift` gets exactly one vector to cover an English present and a German poison, and no amount of cross-lingual training fixes that, because the information needed to resolve it was never in the input. English usually wins — it is most of the training data — so the margin is more interesting than the winner. The exceptions are the best part: two of the models read `kind` as the German for child, and the most strongly aligned one reads `gut` as the German for good.

glossary.label: two meanings
glossary.short: A word with more than one sense still gets one vector, so it is stranded between them.
glossary.detail: Watch `python` sit halfway between the snakes and the programming, belonging to neither. This is a property of any model that assigns one vector per string, and it is the same limitation the homograph set shows arriving from a different direction.

glossary.label: vector arithmetic
glossary.short: king − man + woman, done on the vectors, and what the result lands nearest to.
glossary.detail: It genuinely works on GloVe — `queen` comes back at 0.69 — because GloVe is the kind of model it was discovered on. It is much weaker on a contrastively trained sentence encoder, so a miss there is a property of the model rather than a bug. The per-term similarities are shown because when an analogy fails the usual reason is that the result never left the term it started from.

glossary.label: candidate pool
glossary.short: The words an answer was allowed to come from. GloVe searches all 50,000; the others search only what you have indexed.
glossary.detail: This changes what an answer means, so it is printed next to every one. `queen` from GloVe is a real claim: it is the nearest point in the whole space. The nearest word from a model with no local vocabulary is only the nearest of the words you happen to have added, which is a much weaker claim. Seeding the index is what makes the second closer to the first.

glossary.label: no vector
glossary.short: A word the model has no entry for. Shown dashed rather than silently dropped.
glossary.detail: GloVe is a fixed 50,000-word English list from 2014, so it has nothing for `kubernetes`, and nothing for 28 of the 48 words in the translations grid. A vocabulary has a cutoff date like anything else. Where too much of a word set is missing, the alignment report refuses to score it rather than returning a flattering number computed over the words that survived.
